Fast-Moving Cold Front

Fast-moving cold fronts are pushed by intense pressure systems far behind the actual front. [Figure 4-7] The friction between the ground and the cold front retards the movement of the front and creates a steeper frontal surface. This results in a very narrow band of weather concentrated along the leading edge of the front. If the warm air being overtaken by the cold front is relatively stable, overcast skies and rain may occur for some distance ahead of the front. If the warm air is unstable, scattered thunderstorms and rain showers may form. A continuous line of thunderstorms, or squall line, may form along or ahead of the front. Squall lines present a serious hazard to pilots as squall type thunderstorms are intense and move quickly. Behind a fast-moving cold front, the skies usually clear rapidly and the front leaves behind gusty, turbulent winds and colder temperatures.

Glossary

AMPHIBIAN—A seaplane with retractable wheel-type landing gear that can be extended to allow landings to be made on land.

ANCHOR—A heavy hook connected to the seaplane by a line or cable, intended to dig into the bottom and keep the seaplane from drifting.

AUXILIARY FIN — An additional vertical stabilizer installed on some float planes to offset the increased surface area of the floats in front of the center of gravity.

BEACHING—Pulling a seaplane up onto a suitable shore so that its weight is supported by relatively dry ground rather than water.

BEAUFORT WIND SCALE—A standardized scale ranging from 0-12 correlating the velocity of the wind with predictable surface features of the water.

BILGE—The lowest point inside a float, hull, or watertight compartment.

BILGE PUMP—A pump used to extract water that has leaked into the bilge of a float or flying boat.

BULKHEAD—A structural partition that divides a float or a flying boat hull into separate compartments and provides additional strength.

BUOYANCY—The tendency of a body to float or to rise when submerged in a fluid.

BUOYS—Floating objects moored to the bottom to mark a channel, waterway, or obstruction.

CAN BUOYS—Cylindrical buoys marking the left side of a channel for an inbound vessel. They have odd numbers which increase from seaward.

CAPSIZE—To overturn.

CAST OFF—To release or untie a vessel from its mooring point.

CENTER OF BUOYANCY—The average point of buoyancy in floating objects. Weight added above this point will cause the floating object to sit deeper in the water in a level attitude.

CHINE—The longitudinal seam joining the sides to the bottom of the float. The chines serve a structural purpose, transmitting loads from the bottoms to the sides of the floats. They also serve a hydrodynamic purpose, guiding water away from the float, reducing spray, and contributing to hydrodynamic lift.

CHOP—A roughened condition of the sea surface caused by local winds. It is characterized by its irregularity, short distance between crests, and whitecaps.

COMBINATION SKI—A type of aircraft ski that can be used on snow or ice, but that also allows the use of the skiplane's wheels for landing on runways.

CREST—The top of a wave.

CURRENT — The horizontal movement of a body of water.

DAYBEACONS — Unlighted beacons.

DAYMARKS—Conspicuous markings or shapes that aid in making navigational aids readily visible and easy to identify against daylight viewing backgrounds.

DECK—The top of the float, which can serve as a step or walkway. Bilge pump openings, hand hole covers, and mooring cleats are typically located along the deck.

DISPLACEMENT POSITION—The attitude of the seaplane when its entire weight is supported by the buoyancy of the floats, as it is when at rest or during a slow taxi. Also called the idling position.

DOCK—To secure a seaplane to a permanent structure fixed to the shore. As a noun, the platform or structure to which the seaplane is secured.

DOWNSWELL—Motion in the same direction the swell is moving.

FETCH—An area where wind is generating waves on the water surface. Also the distance the waves have been driven by the wind blowing in a constant direction without obstruction.

FLOATPLANE — A seaplane equipped with separate floats to support the fuselage well above the water surface.

FLOATS—The components of a floatplane's landing gear that provide the buoyancy to keep the airplane afloat.

faqs.question: Why do seaplanes with engines mounted above the fuselage tend to nose down when power is applied?
faqs.answer: Because the thrust line is well above the center of drag, applying power creates a pitching moment that pushes the nose down; reducing power allows the nose to rise.

faqs.question: What additional training is recommended for pilots transitioning to a seaplane with an engine mounted above the fuselage?
faqs.answer: Pilots should receive specific training on the unique handling characteristics of these aircraft, especially the opposite pitch response to power changes, to avoid unexpected pitch changes and dangerous situations.

faqs.question: Which nautical terms are commonly used when operating seaplanes and what do they mean?
faqs.answer: Terms include port (left side), starboard (right side), windward (upwind side), leeward (downwind side), bow (front end), and stern (rear end) of the aircraft or float.

faqs.question: What is the purpose of the keel on a float?
faqs.answer: The keel runs along the center of the float’s bottom, guiding the float straight through the water and resisting sideways motion, similar to a boat’s keel.

faqs.question: What is a skeg and where is it located on a float?
faqs.answer: A skeg is a short, strong extension of the keel located directly behind the step on the float.

faqs.question: What is the chine on a float and what function does it serve?
faqs.answer: The chine is the seam where the sides of the float join the bottom; it helps guide water away from the float, reduces spray, and contributes to hydrodynamic lift.

faqs.question: What are sister keelsons and what do they do?
faqs.answer: Sister keelsons are two longitudinal members positioned midway between the keel and chine on the front portion of the float; they add structural strength and act as additional keels.

faqs.question: What are spray rails and why are they important for seaplanes?
faqs.answer: Spray rails are metal flanges on the inboard forward portions of the chines that reduce the amount of water spray reaching the propeller, protecting it from damage especially at high RPM.

faqs.answer: Floats are rated based on the weight of the volume of fresh water they displace; the displaced fresh‑water weight equals the nominal support capacity of the float.

faqs.question: Why is fresh water used as the standard for float weight rating instead of seawater?
faqs.answer: Fresh water is the standard because seawater is about 3 % denser, allowing it to support more weight; using fresh water provides a consistent, conservative reference for rating.

Because the thrust line sits well above the center of drag, applying power causes the nose to drop, while reducing power makes it rise—opposite to most aircraft and requiring special pilot training. - **Keel**: central longitudinal runner that guides the float and resists sideways motion.
- **Skeg**: short extension of the keel located just behind the step.
- **Chine**: seam where the sides meet the bottom, aiding water shedding and lift.
- **Keelsons**: twin longitudinal members midway between keel and chine that add strength.
- **Deck**: top surface providing cabin access and housing bilge pump openings, hand‑hole covers, and mooring cleats.
- **Rubber bumper**: cushions minor impacts at the float front.
- **Spray rails**: metal flanges on the inboard forward chine that reduce water spray reaching the propeller.

Floats are rated by the weight of fresh water they can displace; since seawater is about 3 % denser, it can support slightly more weight. For example, a float displacing 2,500 lb of fresh water can nominally support 2,500 lb. Large‑diameter conductors may need reshaping after cutting. All insulation must be removed to expose the bare conductor before making electrical connections. Copper wires can be stripped with a variety of tools; Figure 4‑107 lists recommended strippers for different sizes and insulation types. Aluminum wire requires extra care because its strands fracture easily when nicked.

General stripping precautions include:

2. Adjust automatic strippers per the manufacturer’s instructions, especially for aluminum and copper smaller than No. 10, to avoid nicking.
3. Inspect stripped wires; re‑strip or replace any that exceed the allowable number of damaged strands.
4. Ensure the cut insulation edge is clean, trimming if necessary.
5. Remove all insulation, including any transparent inner layer.
6. For lengths over ¼ inch, strip in multiple passes.
7. Retwist copper strands by hand or with pliers to restore lay.

Splicing should be minimized, especially in high‑vibration areas. When splices are required, they should be placed where periodic inspection is possible and staggered to avoid excessive bundle enlargement. Preferred splice connectors are self‑insulated; non‑insulated connectors may be used if covered with plastic sleeving. Solder splices are discouraged due to brittleness. Electrical connections are typically made with solderless terminal lugs, allowing easy attachment to terminal blocks, bus bars, or other equipment. These lugs and splices are made of copper or aluminum and may be pre‑insulated or bare, depending on the application.

Chapter 4: Weather Theory & Reports

Introduction

Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a given time and place, with respect to temperature, moisture content, stability, visibility, and cloudiness. These factors interact to form the following five major meteorological elements:

  • Atmospheric pressure (high or low).
  • Wind (calm or storm).
  • Clouds (clearness or cloudiness).
  • Precipitation (rain, sleet, snow).

A solid understanding of weather theory provides the tools necessary to understand the reports and forecasts obtained from a Flight Service Station (FSS) weather specialist and other aviation weather services. No other means of aviation relies more heavily on knowledge and understanding of weather for its safety than ballooning. It is important to note, however, that there is no substitute for experience.

There are many excellent texts and online sources available for learning more about weather that are referenced at the appropriate point in this chapter. Much of the following information can be found in the Aviation Weather Handbook FAA-H-8083-28, which may be found on the FAA's website.

Other online sources for weather information are also helpful. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) offers a weather tutorial. Developed to meet the needs of educators, weather professionals, and others interested in learning more about weather, it provides a number of concise explanations of weather theory. Additionally, there is a site developed as part of the Weather World 2010 project by the Department of Atmospheric Sciences at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.

This chapter is designed to give balloon pilots a basic knowledge of weather principles, acquaint them with the weather information available for flight planning, and help them develop sound decision-making skills as they prepare for and execute a safe flight.

The Atmosphere

The atmosphere is the envelope of air that surrounds the Earth. Approximately one-half of the air, by weight, is within the lower 18,000 feet. The remainder of the air is spread over a vertical distance in excess of 1,000 miles. No definite outer atmospheric boundary exists, but the air particles become less numerous with increasing altitude until they gradually overcome Earth's gravity and escape into space. In addition to the rotation of the air with the rotation of the Earth, another type of air movement occurs within the atmosphere. This movement of air around the surface of the Earth is called atmospheric circulation.

Composition

The atmosphere is a blanket of air composed of a mixture of gases that surrounds the Earth and reaches over 560 kilometers (km), 348 miles, from the surface. This blanket of gases provides protection from ultraviolet rays, as well as supporting human, animal, and plant life. Nitrogen accounts for 78 percent of the gases comprising the atmosphere, while oxygen makes up 21 percent. [Figure 4-1] Argon, carbon dioxide, and traces of other gases make up the remaining 1 percent. Within this envelope of gases, there are several recognizable layers of the atmosphere as defined by altitude.

topics.context: 1. Decrease in lift due to the direction of the lifting force. 2. Excessive rudder inputs as a result of reduced flight control pressures. 3. The normal stability and inherent characteristics of the airplane to nose-down with the power off. These three factors make it necessary to use more back pressure on the elevator than is required for a straight glide or a level turn, and they have an effect on control coordination. The rudder compensates for yawing tendencies when rolling in or out of a gliding turn; however, the required rudder pedal pressures are reduced as a result of the reduced forces acting on the control surfaces. A learner may apply excessive rudder pedal pressures based on experience with powered flight. This overcontrol of the aircraft may cause slips and skids and result in potentially hazardous flight control conditions. Some examples of this hazard are: • A low-level gliding steep turn during an engine failure emergency. If the rudder is excessively deflected in the direction of the bank while the pilot is increasing elevator back pressure in an attempt to retain altitude, the situation can rapidly turn into an unrecoverable spin. • During a power-off landing approach. The pilot depresses the rudder pedal with excessive pressure that leads to increased lift on the outside wing, banking the airplane in the direction of the rudder deflection. The pilot may improperly apply the opposite aileron to prevent the bank from increasing while applying elevator back pressure. If allowed to progress, this situation may result in a fully developed cross-control condition. A stall in this situation almost certainly results in a rapid and unrecoverable spin. Level-off from a glide is really two different maneuvers depending on the type of glide: • First, in the event of a complete power failure, the best glide speed should be held until necessary to reconfigure for the landing. The pilot should plan for a steeper approach than usual. A 10 percent lead (100 feet if the descent rate is 1,000 feet per minute) factor should be sufficient to slow the descent before landing. • Second, in the case of simulated power failure training, power should be applied as the 10 percent lead value appears on the altimeter. This allows a slow but positive power application to maintain or increase airspeed while the pilot raises the nose to stop the descent and re-trims the airplane as necessary. The level-off from a practice glide should be started before reaching the desired altitude because of the airplane's downward inertia. The amount of lead depends on the rate of descent and the desired airspeed upon completion of the level off. For example, assume the aircraft is in a 500 fpm rate of descent, and the desired final airspeed is higher than the glide speed. The altitude lead should begin at approximately 100 feet above the target altitude. At the lead point, power should be increased to the appropriate level flight cruise power setting. The airplane's nose tends to rise as airspeed and power increase, and the pilot should smoothly control the pitch attitude such that the level-off is completed at the desired altitude and airspeed. When recovery is being made from a gliding turn to a normal glide, the back pressure on the elevator control, which was applied during the turn, needs to be decreased or the airplane may pitch up and experience a loss of airspeed. This error requires considerable attention and conscious control adjustment to re-establish a normal glide airspeed. Common errors in the performance of descents and descending turns are: 1. Failure to adequately clear for aircraft traffic in the turn direction or descent. 2. Inadequate elevator back pressure during glide entry resulting in an overly steep glide. 3. Failure to slow the airplane to approximate glide speed prior to lowering pitch attitude. 4. Attempting to establish/maintain a normal glide solely by reference to flight instruments. 5. Inability to sense changes in airspeed through sound and feel. 6. Inability to stabilize the glide (chasing the airspeed indicator). 7. Attempting to “stretch” the glide by applying back-elevator pressure. 8. Skidding or slipping during gliding turns and not recognizing the difference in rudder forces with and without power. 9. Failure to lower pitch attitude during gliding turn entry resulting in a decrease in airspeed. 10. Excessive rudder pressure during recovery from gliding turns. 11. Inadequate pitch control during recovery from straight glide. 12. Cross-controlling during gliding turns near the ground. 13. Failure to maintain constant bank angle during gliding turns.

sentiment.summary: Describes lift loss, excessive rudder use, and control errors during glides, outlining hazards, corrective procedures, and common mistakes for safe power‑off flight.

faqs.question: Why is additional back‑pressure on the elevator required during a power‑off glide or a gliding turn?
faqs.answer: When the engine is off the lift decreases because the lift vector is no longer aligned with the flight path, and the airplane naturally tends to nose‑down. Reduced rudder forces also mean the pilot may use excessive rudder. To keep the nose up and maintain the desired glide path, more elevator back‑pressure is needed than in a straight glide or level turn.

faqs.question: What hazards can result from applying excessive rudder pedal pressure during a gliding turn?
faqs.answer: Excessive rudder can cause the aircraft to slip or skid, leading to cross‑control conditions. In a steep, low‑level gliding turn this can quickly develop into an unrecoverable spin, especially if the pilot also adds too much elevator back‑pressure.

faqs.question: How should a pilot execute a level‑off from a glide after a complete power failure?
faqs.answer: The pilot should hold best‑glide speed until the altitude lead point is reached (about 10 % of the descent rate, e.g., 100 ft for a 1 000 fpm descent). Then, with a smooth increase of power, raise the nose to stop the descent and re‑trim the aircraft, completing the level‑off at the desired altitude and airspeed.

faqs.question: What is the recommended altitude lead for a level‑off when the descent rate is 500 fpm and a higher final airspeed is desired?
faqs.answer: Begin the power increase about 100 ft above the target altitude. This provides enough lead to raise the nose, increase airspeed, and complete the level‑off without overshooting.

faqs.question: What are common errors pilots make during descents and gliding turns?
faqs.answer: Typical errors include: failing to clear traffic, using insufficient elevator back‑pressure on entry, not slowing to glide speed before lowering pitch, relying only on instruments, not sensing airspeed changes by feel, chasing the airspeed indicator, overstretching the glide with back‑elevator, slipping or skidding without recognizing rudder force changes, not lowering pitch on entry, applying excessive rudder on recovery, inadequate pitch control on recovery, cross‑controlling near the ground, and not maintaining a constant bank angle.

faqs.question: How can a pilot avoid a cross‑control condition during a power‑off gliding turn?
faqs.answer: By using appropriate, reduced rudder pressure that matches the lower forces on the control surfaces, coordinating aileron and rudder inputs, and decreasing elevator back‑pressure when transitioning from a turn to a straight glide to prevent the nose from pitching up excessively.

faqs.question: What should a pilot do if the airplane pitches up after recovering from a gliding turn?
faqs.answer: The pilot must consciously reduce elevator back‑pressure to prevent the nose from rising too much, which could cause a loss of airspeed and a potential stall.

faqs.question: Why might a learner apply too much rudder during a power‑off glide?
faqs.answer: Learners often rely on their experience from powered flight, where higher rudder pressures are needed. In a glide the forces are reduced, so applying the same pressure can lead to over‑control, slips, skids, and hazardous flight conditions.

faqs.question: What is the effect of “stretching” the glide by applying excessive back‑elevator pressure?
faqs.answer: Stretching the glide increases the nose‑up attitude, which reduces airspeed and can cause the aircraft to descend faster than intended, increasing the risk of a stall or spin, especially near the ground.

faqs.question: How does reduced lift direction affect the airplane’s stability during a glide?
faqs.answer: The lift vector points more forward than upward, decreasing overall lift and causing the airplane to naturally nose‑down. This reduces the effectiveness of the rudder and requires more elevator back‑pressure to maintain glide path and attitude.

summary.title: Hazards and Common Errors in Power‑Off Gliding Maneuvers
summary.long_summary:
When an aircraft is gliding without power, three aerodynamic factors increase pilot workload: reduced lift due to the direction of the lift vector, diminished control‑surface pressures that lead to excessive rudder inputs, and the airplane’s natural tendency to nose‑down when power is off. To maintain altitude or a level turn, pilots must apply more elevator back pressure than in a straight glide, and they must coordinate rudder use carefully. Inexperienced pilots often over‑apply rudder based on powered‑flight habits, creating slips, skids, and hazardous cross‑control situations. Specific scenarios include a low‑level steep turn during an engine‑failure emergency, where excessive rudder and back‑elevator can precipitate an unrecoverable spin, and a power‑off landing approach, where too much rudder deflection raises lift on the outside wing, inducing a bank that, if corrected with opposite aileron and continued back‑pressure, can evolve into a full cross‑control stall and spin.

Level‑off from a glide differs for true power failures versus simulated training. In a real failure, the pilot should hold best‑glide speed until a 10 % altitude lead (e.g., 100 ft for a 1,000 fpm descent) allows a steeper approach and safe touchdown. In training, power is reapplied at the lead point to raise airspeed and pitch while trimming for level flight. Errors commonly observed during descents and gliding turns include failure to clear traffic, insufficient elevator back pressure on entry, not reducing speed before lowering pitch, reliance solely on instruments, inability to sense airspeed changes, over‑stretching the glide with back‑elevator, skidding or slipping without recognizing altered rudder forces, and excessive rudder during recovery. Proper awareness of these factors and disciplined control inputs are essential to prevent spins and maintain safe gliding performance.

Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) governs Aeronautics and Space. Chapter 1, administered by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) within the Department of Transportation, is organized into multiple subchapters that address distinct regulatory areas. 

- **Subchapter A** covers definitions and general requirements, including Part 1 (definitions and abbreviations). 
- **Subchapter B** sets procedural rules such as Part 11 (general rulemaking procedures) and Part 17 (protests and contract disputes). 
- **Subchapter C** focuses on aircraft, detailing certification procedures (Part 21), airworthiness standards for various aircraft categories (Parts 23‑31), airworthiness directives (Part 39), maintenance and alteration rules (Part 43), and identification/registration marking (Part 45). 
- **Subchapter D** pertains to airmen, including pilot and instructor certification (Part 61), medical standards (Part 67), and provisions for operating certain small aircraft without a medical certificate (Part 68). 
- **Subchapter E** defines airspace classifications and special use airspace (Parts 71 and 73). 
- **Subchapter F** outlines air traffic and general operating rules (Part 91) and related procedures (Parts 97, 103). 
- Subsequent subchapters address air carriers (G), schools and certificated agencies (H), airports (I), navigational facilities (J), and administrative regulations (K). 

The accompanying bullet points highlight four critical parts: 
- **Part 21** establishes procedures for issuing airworthiness certificates and approvals; a standard airworthiness certificate (FAA Form 8100‑2) must be displayed on the aircraft and remains valid when the aircraft conforms to its approved type design and is maintained per Parts 21, 43, and 91. 
- **Part 39** authorizes the FAA to issue Airworthiness Directives (ADs) when unsafe conditions are identified that could affect the same type design. 
- **Part 43** governs maintenance, rebuilding, and alteration of U.S.-certificated aircraft, covering airframes, engines, propellers, and components. 
- **Part 45** sets requirements for identification and registration markings on aircraft, engines, propellers, and certain parts. 

Together, these subchapters and parts provide a comprehensive regulatory framework for aircraft certification, operation, maintenance, and safety within the United States.

Rotor winds are associated with mountainous terrain and strong winds aloft. Mountain flights should anticipate rotor winds, and in particular, when wind aloft forecasts exceed 15 knots at mountain peak altitude. Prediction of rotor winds is not a well developed science. summary.title: Rotor Winds and Balloon Flight Hazards in Mountainous Terrain
summary.long_summary: Rotor winds occur over mountainous terrain when strong winds aloft—typically exceeding 15 knots at the peak elevation—interact with the terrain. These winds can generate a downward‑flowing rotor zone whose forces often surpass a balloon’s performance envelope, even when the envelope is at its red‑line temperature. The downward airflow can force the balloon to the ground, and escaping a rotor is difficult; the primary method of escape is to climb through the top of the rotor. The vertical component of the rotor can actually aid ascent: a strong climb rate on the rotor’s upslope can propel the balloon out of the rotor by inertia. Once the rotor area is identified, pilots can avoid it by maintaining an altitude roughly 3,000–4,000 feet above the highest terrain. Although rotor zones are sometimes completely calm, they are frequently turbulent and represent a serious hazard that can outweigh the scenic appeal of mountain flying. Balloonists planning mountain flights should therefore anticipate rotor winds, monitor wind‑aloft forecasts, and plan routes that stay well above the identified rotor zones.

USE THE RESTRAINT SYSTEM... PROPERLY

Federal regulations1 require that safety belts and shoulder harnesses (when installed) be properly worn during landings and takeoffs. If the restraint is not worn properly, it cannot provide full benefits and can even cause injury in a serious impact.

Tests have shown that slack in the restraint system should be minimal. In an impact, your body keeps moving until the slack is taken out of the restraint, but then must be abruptly stopped to “catch up” with the airplane. The restraint should be adjusted as tightly as your comfort will permit to minimize potential injuries.

The safety belt should be placed low on your hipbones so that the belt loads will be taken by the strong skeleton of your body. If the safety belt is improperly positioned on your abdomen, it can cause internal injuries. If the safety belt is positioned on your thighs, rather than the hipbones, it cannot effectively limit your body’s forward motion.

Shoulder harness systems can use dual shoulder belts or a single diagonal belt similar to those used in automobiles. The belts should not rub against your head or neck. This is uncomfortable, will discourage use of the shoulder harness, and can also cause neck injuries during an impact.

Single diagonal shoulder belts should be positioned so that the torso’s center of gravity falls within the angle formed by the shoulder belt and the safety belt. Otherwise your torso may roll right out of the shoulder belt during an impact and compromise your protection.

Because the lower end of the shoulder belt is usually fastened to the safety belt buckle or the buckle insert, the safety belt buckle should be positioned on the side of your hip. This differs from the central location of the buckle that is common when only the safety belt is used.

Be sure that the safety belt is installed so that when the buckle is unlatched, both the safety belt and the shoulder belt are released. Also, be sure that the buckle can be unlatched without interference from the seat armrest, aircraft controls, or the interior wall of the airplane.

If the shoulder harness uses dual belts fastened to the safety belt near the center of your body, the shoulder belts will tend to pull the safety belt off your hip bones. This could cause internal injuries in an impact.

When it is tightened about your hips, the safety belt should be positioned so that it makes an angle of about 55 degrees with the centerline of the airplane.

This allows it to resist the upward pull of the shoulder belts, reducing the risk of internal injury.

faqs.answer: The safety belt should be placed low on the hipbones so the load is taken by the strong skeleton of the hips.

faqs.question: What can happen if the safety belt is positioned on the abdomen or thighs?
faqs.answer: If placed on the abdomen, the belt can cause internal injuries; if placed on the thighs, it cannot effectively limit forward motion.

faqs.question: How should a single diagonal shoulder belt be positioned to keep the torso protected?
faqs.answer: The torso’s center of gravity should fall within the angle formed by the diagonal shoulder belt and the safety belt; otherwise the torso may roll out of the belt during impact.

faqs.question: Why must shoulder belts not rub against the head or neck?
faqs.answer: Rubbing against the head or neck is uncomfortable, discourages use, and can cause neck injuries during an impact.

faqs.question: Where should the safety‑belt buckle be located when a shoulder harness is used?
faqs.answer: The buckle should be positioned on the side of the hip, not in the central location used when only a safety belt is worn.

faqs.question: What should be ensured about the buckle’s release mechanism?
faqs.answer: When the buckle is unlatched, both the safety belt and the shoulder belt must be released, and the release should not be obstructed by the seat armrest, aircraft controls, or interior wall.

faqs.question: What angle should the safety belt make with the airplane’s centerline when tightened around the hips?
faqs.answer: The safety belt should make an angle of about 55 degrees with the airplane’s centerline, allowing it to resist the upward pull of the shoulder belts and reduce the risk of internal injury.

summary.title: Proper Use of Aircraft Restraint Systems
summary.long_summary: Federal regulations require safety belts and shoulder harnesses to be properly worn during takeoff and landing. The restraint must be snug; any slack reduces protection and can cause injury in an impact. The belt should sit low on the hipbones so the load is transferred to the strong skeletal structure; placement on the abdomen can cause internal injuries, and positioning on the thighs fails to limit forward motion. Shoulder harnesses may use dual shoulder belts or a single diagonal belt; they must not rub the head or neck. For a diagonal belt, the torso’s center of gravity must fall within the angle formed by the shoulder and safety belts, otherwise the torso can roll out during impact. The safety‑belt buckle should be on the side of the hip, not centrally, when a shoulder harness is used, and both belts must release together without obstruction from armrests, controls, or the aircraft interior. Dual belts fastened near the body’s center can pull the safety belt off the hips, increasing injury risk. When tightened around the hips, the belt should form roughly a 55‑degree angle with the aircraft’s centerline to resist upward pull from the shoulder belts and reduce internal injury risk.

summary.title: AME Procedures for Pilots Reporting Recent DUI
summary.long_summary: When a pilot informs an Aviation Medical Examiner (AME) of a DUI conviction or administrative action within the past five years, the AME must follow several mandatory steps. The Office of Aerospace Medicine requires the AME to act within 14 days for initial assessment and within 60 days to complete required reporting. FAA security rules (AXE‑700) obligate the pilot to notify the Security and Hazardous Materials Safety Office of any DUI/DWI conviction or administrative action, and the AME must ensure the notification letter is submitted within 60 days of the event. The AME must collect an Alcohol Event Status Report, which includes the airman's statement on current alcohol/drug use, BAC results (BAC > .15 must be deferred to the FAA), court or police reports, driving record, and evidence of treatment. Even if the DUI is older than 60 days, the pilot must still submit the notification to Security. A refusal to undergo testing is treated as a positive result. All actions are mandated by 14 CFR §61.15.

SUBJ: Operational Data Reporting Requirements

  1. Purpose of this Order. This order establishes reporting requirements and procedures for collecting air traffic activity counts and delay data through the Air Traffic Operations Network (OPSNET).
  2. Audience. This order applies to the following Air Traffic Organization (ATO) service units: Air Traffic Services, Terminal, and System Operations Services; Service Center offices; and all air traffic control (ATC) field facilities, excluding flight service stations (FSS).
  3. Where Can I Find This Order? This order is available on the MY FAA employee Web site https://employees.faa.gov/tools_resources/orders_notices/ and the air traffic publications Web site at http://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications.
  4. Cancellation. This order cancels Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Order JO 7210.55F, Operational Data Reporting Requirements dated October 1, 2009.
  5. Background. OPSNET was created in 1988 to replace the portion of the National Airspace Performance Reporting System responsible for the collection of delay and traffic count data. In 1999, the OPSNET software was redesigned to provide additional capabilities for entering data and to expand the data-reporting program to additional facilities. In October 2004, both the format and method for entering OPSNET data were updated by implementing an Internet application, OPSNET Web. AutoOPSNET phase 1 of this approach, implemented on October 22, 2007, automated the data entry for EDCT delays for GDP, AFP and GS. Phase 2 of this approach, effective October 1, 2008, automated the data entry for all airborne delays.
  6. Explanation of Change. This Order has been updated to replace the Office of System Efficiency with the Office of Performance Analysis. The remainder of the order has been updated to accurately reflect program roles and responsibilities and add the TFMS Production Center.
